edges.effect_quant: Pregnancy causes large, trimester-specific shifts in thyroid physiology rather than a one-directional linear effect. One cohort found TSH reference intervals of 0.18 to 2.99 mIU/L at 9 to 12 weeks, 0.11 to 3.98 in the second trimester, and 0.48 to 4.71 in the third, while both low and high maternal thyroid hormone availability have been linked to adverse outcomes in observational cohorts and meta-analytic work.
edges.population: pregnant women across the trimesters of gestation
edges.mechanism: Human chorionic gonadotropin stimulates the thyroid early in pregnancy and can suppress TSH, while rising thyroxine-binding globulin, altered iodine demand, placental deiodinase activity, and fetal dependence on maternal hormone shift thyroid homeostasis over time. The result is a dynamic physiologic curve in which both low and high thyroid hormone availability can become problematic.
edges.summary: Pregnancy has a strong and distinctly trimester-dependent effect on thyroid function, making a u-shaped interpretation the best fit. Early gestation tends to lower TSH and alter free thyroid hormone measurements, then reference ranges shift again later in pregnancy, and both ends of the thyroid-function spectrum have been associated with adverse maternal or child outcomes.
edges.caveats: This edge is about physiologic and clinical thyroid-function shifts during pregnancy, not a claim that pregnancy itself is a disease exposure. Assay differences, iodine status, ethnicity, body size, and local population reference intervals materially affect what should be considered normal.
